content: Interpreting the results of genotypic resistance tests requires a comprehensive understanding of the mutations selected by various antiretroviral (ARV) drugs and the potential for cross-resistance to other drugs conferred by specific mutations. The International AIDS Society-USA (IAS-USA) maintains an updated list of significant resistance-associated mutations in the reverse transcriptase (RT), protease (PR), integrase (IN), and envelope genes. Additionally, the Stanford University HIV Drug Resistance Database provides valuable guidance for interpreting genotypic resistance test results. Various tools are now available to assist clinicians in interpreting these results effectively. Clinical trials have demonstrated that consulting with specialists in HIV drug resistance improves virologic outcomes. Therefore, clinicians are encouraged to seek expert consultation when interpreting genotypic test results and designing optimal new treatment regimens. Phenotypic assays measure the ability of a virus to replicate in the presence of varying concentrations of ARV drugs. These assays involve inserting RT, PR, integrase, or envelope gene sequences derived from patient plasma HIV RNA into the backbone of a laboratory clone of HIV or using them to generate pseudotyped viruses that express the patient-derived HIV genes of interest. The replication of these viruses at different drug concentrations is monitored using a reporter gene and compared to the replication of a reference HIV strain. Automated phenotypic assays, which can produce results within 2 to 3 weeks, are commercially available but are more expensive than genotypic assays. These assays provide fold resistance values (e.g., fold increase in IC50) associated with drug failure, although clinically significant fold increase cutoffs are now available for some drugs. Consulting with a specialist to interpret these results can be beneficial. Both genotypic and phenotypic assays have limitations, including the lack of uniform quality assurance testing for all available assays, relatively high costs, and insensitivity to minor viral species. Drug-resistant viruses that constitute less than 10% to 20% of the circulating viral population are unlikely to be detected by commercially available assays. This limitation is significant because wild-type virus often reemerges as the predominant population in plasma after selective pressure from ARV drugs is removed. Consequently, the proportion of virus with resistance mutations decreases below the detection threshold of 10% to 20%. For some drugs, this reversion to predominantly wild-type virus can occur within 4 to 6 weeks after discontinuation of the drugs. Prospective clinical studies have shown that despite this plasma reversion, re-initiation of the same ARV agents (or those sharing similar resistance pathways) is usually associated with early drug failure, and the virus present at failure is derived from previously archived resistant virus. Therefore, resistance testing is most valuable when performed before or within 4 weeks after discontinuation of ARV drugs. In some cases, resistance testing done 4 to 6 weeks after drug discontinuation may still detect mutations, but the absence of detectable resistance must be interpreted cautiously when designing subsequent ARV regimens. The use of resistance assays in clinical practice is critical for determining initial treatment strategies. Transmission of drug-resistant HIV strains is well-documented and is associated with suboptimal virologic responses to initial antiretroviral therapy (ART). The risk of acquiring drug-resistant virus is related to the prevalence of drug resistance in HIV-infected individuals engaging in high-risk behaviors within a given community. In regions such as the United States, some European countries, Australia, and Japan, approximately 10% to 17% of ART-naïve patients have resistance mutations to at least one ARV drug. Up to 8%, but generally less than 5%, of transmitted viruses exhibit resistance to drugs from more than one class. Transmitted resistant HIV is most commonly resistant to nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitors (NRTIs) or non-nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitors (NNRTIs), while protease inhibitor (PI) resistance is less common, and transmitted integrase strand transfer inhibitor (INSTI) resistance is rare. In individuals with acute or recent (early) HIV infection, resistance testing can guide therapy selection to optimize virologic response. Resistance testing in this context is recommended, and a genotypic assay is preferred for this purpose. Treatment initiation should not be delayed while awaiting resistance testing results if the patient is willing and able to begin therapy. Once results are available, the regimen can be modified if necessary. In the absence of ART, resistant viruses may decline over time to levels below the detection limit of standard resistance tests. However, even low levels of resistant viruses may increase the risk of treatment failure when ART is eventually initiated. Therefore, if ART is deferred, resistance testing should still be performed during acute HIV infection, and the genotypic resistance test result should be kept on record until the patient begins ART. Interpreting drug-resistance testing before ART initiation in patients with chronic HIV infection is more complex. The rate at which transmitted resistance-associated mutations revert to wild-type virus has not been fully delineated, but mutations present at the time of HIV transmission are more stable than those selected under drug pressure. Resistance-associated mutations in viruses transmitted several years earlier can often still be detected. Although no prospective trial has directly addressed whether drug-resistance testing before therapy initiation provides benefit in this population, data from several studies suggest that virologic responses in individuals with baseline resistance mutations are suboptimal.
